rationale: B wins by a nose because it finds the cleanest non-announcement story in the update: "The new enterprise question: which AI agents get write access?" and adds the overlooked pricing angle, "Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost, including Airtable." A is more disciplined on competitor hallucinations, but it pads the reliability issue into "employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong," which the facts do not earn. B still needs a hard fact scrub; "bets the company" is PR caffeine, not evidence.
gaps_in_A: "employees are the ones left to catch what they get wrong" invents the absence of approvals, human review, or guardrails. The update says reliability data is not disclosed, not that employees are abandoned with the cleanup.
"send communications" overstates the fact pattern. The update says agents can draft emails; drafting is not sending.
The workplace angle is mostly the reliability angle wearing a different hat. Without a customer workflow, admin view, or employee account, it is padded duplicate territory.
It misses the standalone pricing/business-model story. "Pricing for the agent features not finalized" is not just a footnote under reliability; it is its own beat for SaaS monetization reporters.
gaps_in_B: "Airtable, Notion, Smartsheet and Monday" imports competitor context not supplied in the update. Useful in real life, but this judging brief did not give you those facts.
"bets the company on agents" overclaims. The update supports a repositioning and launch, not an existential company wager.
"Nobody has settled on what an AI agent should cost" turns Airtable's unfinalized pricing into a market-wide conclusion without evidence. Nice headline, unsupported spine.
"established category leader" is not in the facts. "Serves many enterprise teams" does not buy you category-leader status.
